summary: A report from the Internet Architecture Board on the role of the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF), on its own and in relation to the IETF. It grew out of IAB discussion while a new IRTF chair was being appointed. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The IRTF runs research groups that study Internet problems without writing standards, and the IETF writes the standards. RFC 4440 is the Internet Architecture Board's account of why that split exists, what the IRTF should be doing, and how the two should work together.

subtitle: The Internet Architecture Board's view of what long-term research should look like, and how it relates to standards work.

today: RFC 4440 is an Informational report from March 2006 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It records the Internet Architecture Board's view of the IRTF at that time and leaves several questions open, including how research groups should contribute on network architecture and whether their output needs a publication track of its own.

sections.title: Why the IAB Wrote This
sections.content:
As part of the process of appointing a new chair of the Internet Research Task Force, the Internet Architecture Board considered the future role of the IRTF both on its own and in relation to the IETF. The IAB expanded that discussion into this report and circulated it for wider community review. As one result of the discussion, Aaron Falk was appointed the new chair of the IRTF in March 2005.

The document is a report on how the two bodies should divide the work, and it is deliberately a discussion rather than a set of rules. Its authors describe it as a more wide-ranging discussion of the possible roles of the IRTF, and note that it is not a revision of RFC 2014, which sets out how research groups operate, but a look at what they are for.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet Architecture Board oversees the IETF, and it appoints the chair of the IRTF. Choosing a new IRTF chair in 2005 made the board ask what the IRTF should be doing, and this document is its answer.

sections.title: How the IRTF and the IETF Came to Be
sections.content:
Before 1989 the IAB, then called the Internet Activities Board, oversaw a number of task forces. In 1989 organisational changes coalesced those task forces into two groups. The IRTF was tasked to consider long-term research problems in the Internet, and the IETF to concentrate on short- to medium-term engineering issues related to the Internet. At that time all of the task forces except the IETF were restructured as IRTF research groups: the End-to-End Task Force became the End-to-End Research Group, and the Privacy and Security Task Force became the Privacy and Security Research Group.

Much of the early participation in both the IETF and the IRTF came from the academic and research communities. Looking at the membership of the IAB from the 1980s and early 1990s shows members from institutions such as MIT, UCLA, BBN, UCL and SDSC, while members in more recent years were more likely to list companies such as Cisco, IBM, Microsoft, Nokia, Qualcomm and Verisign. The IRTF has continued to have significant academic participation, while the IETF has focused on standards development and become dominated by the needs of the commercial sector.

The IRTF has generally focused on investigation of areas not considered sufficiently mature for IETF standardisation, as well as areas that are not the specific subject of standardisation but could guide future standards work. The IRTF Research Group guidelines and procedures are described in RFC 2014. The IRTF Chair is appointed by the IAB and charters research groups in consultation with the Internet Research Steering Group and with approval of the IAB. The chairs of the research groups make up the main part of that steering group, though the IRTF Chair can also appoint members to it at large.

The past IRTF chairs were Dave Clark from 1989 to 1992, Jon Postel from 1992 to 1995, Abel Weinrib from 1995 to 1999, Erik Huizer from 1999 to 2001, and Vern Paxson from 2001 to 2005.
sections.plainLanguage: Until 1989 the IAB ran task forces directly. That year they were split in two: one group for writing standards in the next few years, and one for research on longer-term questions. The research side has stayed close to universities; the standards side has become dominated by commercial interests.

sections.title: What Makes a Research Group Different
sections.content:
Two key differences separate IRTF research groups from IETF working groups: research groups are not trying to produce standards of any kind, and their output does not require consensus within the group or broad consensus from the IETF.

As RFC 2014 puts it, the IRTF does not set standards. A technology developed in a research group can be brought to the IETF for possible standardisation, but research group input carries no more weight than other community input and goes through the same standards setting process as any other proposal. That is necessary to ensure research groups do not become part of the standards process itself. RFC 2014 also says that since the products are research results rather than Internet standards, consensus of the group is not required. The NameSpace Research Group was one group that did require consensus decisions, because it was chartered exclusively to make a recommendation to the IETF.

Research groups also should not block other work. Unless the IESG clearly specifies otherwise, research groups do not act as gateways controlling the advancement of standards, experimental RFCs or informational RFCs produced by IETF working groups. Nor do existing research groups prevent the creation of new ones in related areas: when considering a proposal for a new research group it is appropriate to consider the relationship with existing groups, but multiple research groups working in the same general area may be formed if appropriate.

Some research groups have acted as minimal-constraint research groups, creating a community for discussing research proposals, with mature proposals tossed over the fence to an IETF group for standardisation. The Reliable Multicast Research Group was an example, with standardisation efforts in the Reliable Multicast Transport working group.
sections.plainLanguage: A research group produces results, not standards. If something it develops looks ready to be standardised, it goes to the IETF and is treated like any other proposal, with no extra weight. A research group also cannot hold up standard work by refusing to let it pass.

sections.title: The Range of Research Groups
sections.content:
The document lists the ways research groups can currently be structured. Membership can be open or closed, as it was for the End-to-End Research Group and the NameSpace Research Group. Groups can be long-term and ongoing, or short-term with a specific goal, as the NameSpace Research Group was chartered to be. RFC 2014, written in 1996, assumed research groups would be long-term, expecting them to have the stable long-term membership needed to promote research collaboration and teamwork.

A group can have a goal of producing proposals for the IETF, as the Anti-Spam Research Group did, or be independent of any current or proposed work in the IETF, as the Delay-Tolerant Networking Research Group was. Activities can include research groups and their meetings, workshops and other one-time activities organised directly by the IRTF, though to date the IRTF has not organised such activities other than in the form of BOFs at IETF meetings. Groups can focus on traditional research, but they can also focus on development, on building tools, on operational testing, on protocol interoperability testing, or on other activities that do not fit the working group model.

The IAB believes the range could be expanded further, in terms of timescale, relationship to the IETF, range of activities, and the range between research and development.
sections.plainLanguage: Research groups are not all the same. Some are open and some are closed, some run for years and some for a fixed goal, some feed proposals into the IETF and some do not, and some do practical work such as testing rather than pure study.

sections.title: Research Groups and Network Architecture
sections.content:
One interest of the IAB is how progress is made on issues of network architecture, which includes developing and evaluating new architectures, understanding the evolving architecture and architectural issues of the decentralised, deployed Internet infrastructure, and building tools for those tasks. The document describes the spectrum of activities for research groups as ranging from the visionary to the specific. Architecture asks where we are and where we go from here. Incubation is where we think we know where to go but do not yet have the tools to get there. Problem focus is where there are specific problems to solve or potential solutions to evaluate.

Where a research group sits on that spectrum depends partly on where the IETF and the field itself lie. In areas such as network management, where the IETF community has doubts about where it should be going, it would be useful for the IETF to look to the IRTF for architectural evaluation. Where the architectural approach is better established, an incubation approach might be more appropriate. Where many pieces of the puzzle are in place but significant problems remain, a problem focus might make sense.

For groups with an architectural focus, it would not be appropriate for the IAB to charter a research group to come up with the architectural perspective on a topic, because any such result would have to pass through the wide feedback and consensus procedures of the IETF. It is appropriate to ask a group for exploration and discussion of an architectural issue, which the IAB has done with the Routing Research Group on research objectives for inter-domain routing improvements. It is also possible for groups to make recommendations on their own initiative, as the End-to-End Research Group and the Crypto Forum Research Group have both done. Some groups work better as a breeding ground for ideas than as a consensus-building community: the NameSpace Research Group, chartered exclusively to make a recommendation to the IETF, never achieved a clear consensus.

The document leaves this open, saying the IAB does not have clear answers on the evolving role of the IRTF in addressing open architectural issues, and that one of its goals is to make more use of the IRTF in investigating architectural issues.
sections.plainLanguage: One thing the board wants from research is help with big architectural questions. A group can study the question and publish what it finds, but it cannot announce the answer: anything that looks like a decision on the architecture has to go through the IETF's own review.

sections.title: The Relationship Between the IETF and the IRTF
sections.content:
For many research groups, part of their value lies in their relationship with the IETF. The document suggests the interchange could be improved in both directions: from the IETF to the IRTF in terms of information about IETF problems that research could help with, and of IETF evaluation of research group efforts; and from the IRTF to the IETF in terms of reports, documents, proposals and BOFs. Current paths for this interchange include IRTF reports at IETF plenary meetings, research group meetings before or after the IETF or in one of the scheduled sessions during it, workshops, and IRTF documents.

One possibility, for some groups rather than all, is for a group to have a design-team-like relationship with the IETF or one of its working groups, with a charter that includes an agreement of deliverables and a time frame. A question that would need resolving is when such a relationship is appropriate for a research group and when a working group should do the work directly.

The document is candid about the limits. Research groups are made of volunteers who choose their own topics, and are usually started by a proposal from individuals who want to form the group, so IRTF activity often will not be viable without people willing to take on the work. While the IETF can request specific research activities, results require individuals within the groups willing to undertake it. Research groups have been of significant benefit to the IETF, with a number of IETF proposals beginning as discussions in the End-to-End Research Group, but the interchange also takes significant time and effort from working group chairs and area directors, sometimes with little to show for it if the group's direction is at odds with what the chairs want.

On the relationship between the research and development communities, the document notes that IRTF participation in the IETF has dropped over the last ten years as the Internet has matured and the difficulty of changing its architecture has grown, and it would be good for research output to reach the IETF somewhat more than it does now. The document also records the discussion about publishing research group output in a venue clearly marked as research rather than as individual submissions, and about decreasing the delay in publishing IRTF RFCs. The security considerations section of the document states that there are none.
sections.plainLanguage: The board wants better traffic in both directions: the IETF telling researchers which problems need solving, and researchers bringing results to the IETF. It also says plainly that research groups depend on volunteers, so a request from the IETF does not guarantee an answer.
